newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech dealers mull cen bank intervention comments.
newsitem.headline: Czech dealers mull cen bank intervention comments.

text.p: The Czech crown held on to early gains on Monday after the central bank said it was not discussing an imminent cut in interest rates and that it would support the currency if the need arose.

Dealers said the CNB's efforts to talk up the crown, after it fell sharply in early Prague trade, had been successful but were left wondering whether, and at what level, the CNB would actually intervene in support.

The crown pulled back to minus 2.9 percent against the mid-point of its mark/dollar fixing basket after CNB board member Ludek Niedermeyer made the remarks from as low as minus 3.8 percent earlier on Monday.
"Of course we stay behind the crown, we are ready to support if necessary and we are following the market very closely," Niedermeyer told Reuters.
Dealers said they took the CNB's remarks about intervention seriously but some thought the central bank would only intervene on the market as a last resort.
"I can imagine that they would go for direct support but it's hard to judge where the target (for intervention) is," said Emil Stava of Citibank.
"I would say that direct intervention (in support) of the Czech crown is the last resort," he added.

The crown can fluctuate 7.5 percent either side of the mid-point of a basket made up of 65 percent marks and 35 percent dollars but many dealers and analysts believe that the CNB operates an unofficial band of plus or minus five percent against the mid-point which it would defend if necessary.
Although the CNB only rarely intervenes directly on the market it often tries to influence the value of the crown by issuing statements clarifying policy.

But Petr Kukla of Girocredit Banka said the power of the CNB to move the market by such methods may diminish and it may have to intervene to prove that its words could be backed by actions if the crown again fell as low as it did early on Monday.
"Next time (the crown falls so low) I think they will intervene. They would have to do it and say 'Now enough talking,'" said Petr Kukla of Girocredit Banka.
The CNB said on Monday that according to preliminary data, its foreign exchange reserves had risen at the end of March to more than $12 billion, from 11.7 billion in February.

The crown has fallen sharply in the last two months driven by worries about the country's overall macroeconomic prospects and a widespread belief that the CNB would heed government calls for a relaxation of monetary policy to boost growth.
However, last Thursday, the CNB ruled out any relaxation of monetary policy in the near term.

Despite the announcement, the crown continued to fall leading some analysts to believe that the crown was becoming less interest rate sensitive and that investors were concentrating on fundamentals, especially the trade deficit.
The Czech Statistical Bureau said last week that March's trade deficit was 13.429 billion crowns compared with 13.415 in February.

Although the figures were around four billion crowns better than expected, Matt Starr, head of treasury at Creditanstalt, said they still implied a current account deficit for 1997 of around eight percent of gross domestic product - one of the biggest deficits in the world.

Last summer, the CNB raised the discount rate to 10.5 percent from 9.5, the Lombard rate to 14 percent from 12.5 percent and bank minimum reserve requirements to 11.5 percent from 8.5. Two weeks ago the CNB cut reserve requirements back to 9.5 percent.
